claim: The crystal structure of the extracellular cysteine rich domain (CRD) of vertebrate Smoothened (Smo) was determined at 2.3 Å resolution.
source: We present the 2.3 Å crystal structure of the extracellular cysteine rich domain (CRD) of vertebrate Smo
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the resolution of the crystal structure, and Table 1 provides detailed crystallographic data showing resolution of 2.3 Å for the SeMet-substituted zSmo CRD.

claim: The Smo CRD binds to oxysterols.
source: We present the 2.3 Å crystal structure of the extracellular cysteine rich domain (CRD) of vertebrate Smo and show that it binds to oxysterols
evidence: The abstract states this finding, and Figures 1D, 2A-E demonstrate binding of the Smo CRD to 20(S)-OHC beads through ligand affinity chromatography experiments.

claim: Oxysterols are endogenous lipids that activate Hedgehog signaling.
source: We present the 2.3 Å crystal structure of the extracellular cysteine rich domain (CRD) of vertebrate Smo and show that it binds to oxysterols, endogenous lipids that activate Hh signaling.
evidence: The abstract makes this claim, supported by Figure 3 showing that 20(S)-OHC activates Gli1 expression and reduces Gli3R levels, and by prior literature citations (Kha et al., 2004; Corcoran and Scott, 2006; Dwyer et al., 2007; Kim et al., 2007; Rohatgi et al., 2007; Johnson et al., 2011).

claim: The oxysterol-binding groove in the Smo CRD is analogous to that used by Frizzled 8 to bind to the palmitoleyl group of Wnt ligands.
source: The oxysterol-binding groove in the Smo CRD is analogous to that used by Frizzled 8 to bind to the palmitoleyl group of Wnt ligands
evidence: The abstract states this, and Figure 6A-B shows structural comparison of the binding grooves in zSmo CRD and Fz8 CRD, with volume calculations demonstrating similar pocket sizes (551 Å³ for zSmo).

claim: The CRD is required for signaling in response to native Hedgehog ligands.
source: The CRD is required for signaling in response to native Hh ligands, showing that it is an important regulatory module for Smo activation.
evidence: The abstract states this claim, and Figure 3A-B demonstrates that ΔCRD-YFP-mSmo fails to activate Gli1 or reduce Gli3R in response to Shh, while retaining responsiveness to SAG.

claim: Targeting of the Smo CRD by oxysterol-inspired small molecules can block signaling by all known classes of Hedgehog activators.
source: Indeed, targeting of the Smo CRD by oxysterol-inspired small molecules can block signaling by all known classes of Hh activators and by clinically relevant Smo mutants.
evidence: The abstract makes this claim, supported by Figure 8A-C showing that 20(R)-yne and 20-keto-yne inhibit signaling induced by SAG, 20(S)-OHC, and Shh.

claim: Oxysterol-based inhibitors can block signaling by clinically relevant Smo mutants.
source: Indeed, targeting of the Smo CRD by oxysterol-inspired small molecules can block signaling by all known classes of Hh activators and by clinically relevant Smo mutants.
evidence: The abstract states this, and Figure 8D-E demonstrates that 20(R)-yne and 20-keto-yne inhibit signaling by mSmo D477H (Vismodegib-resistant mutant) and constitutively active mSmoM2.

claim: The Hedgehog signaling pathway controls the development of many tissues during embryogenesis.
source: The Hedgehog (Hh) signaling pathway controls the development of many tissues during embryogenesis (McMahon et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by the citation to McMahon et al., 2003.

claim: Quantitative abnormalities in Hedgehog signaling can lead to human birth defects.
source: Even quantitative abnormalities in Hh signaling can lead to human birth defects (Bale, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bale, 2002.

claim: After development, Hedgehog signaling regulates tissue stem cells and regenerative responses to injury.
source: After development, Hh signaling regulates tissue stem cells and regenerative responses to injury (Machold et al., 2003; Shin et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Machold et al., 2003 and Shin et al., 2011.

claim: Aberrant Hedgehog signaling can be oncogenic.
source: Aberrant Hh signaling can be oncogenic, and genes encoding Hh pathway proteins can function as oncogenes or tumor suppressor genes (Scales and de Sauvage, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Scales and de Sauvage, 2009.

claim: Patched 1 (Ptch1) is encoded by a tumor suppressor gene.
source: Ptch1, encoded by a tumor suppressor gene, is a 12-pass TM protein that serves as the receptor for Hh ligands, including Sonic Hedgehog (Shh) (Marigo et al., 1996; Stone et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations to Marigo et al., 1996 and Stone et al., 1996.

claim: Patched 1 is a 12-pass transmembrane protein that serves as the receptor for Hedgehog ligands.
source: Ptch1, encoded by a tumor suppressor gene, is a 12-pass TM protein that serves as the receptor for Hh ligands, including Sonic Hedgehog (Shh) (Marigo et al., 1996; Stone et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations to Marigo et al., 1996 and Stone et al., 1996.

claim: Smoothened is a 7-pass transmembrane protein encoded by a human oncogene.
source: In the absence of Hh ligands, Ptch1 inhibits the function of Smo, a 7-pass TM protein that is encoded by a human oncogene.
evidence: This is stated in the text and is established knowledge in the field.

claim: In the absence of Hedgehog ligands, Patched 1 inhibits the function of Smoothened.
source: In the absence of Hh ligands, Ptch1 inhibits the function of Smo, a 7-pass TM protein that is encoded by a human oncogene.
evidence: This is a fundamental mechanism of the Hh pathway, well-established in the literature.

claim: Sonic Hedgehog binds and inactivates Patched 1.
source: Shh binds and inactivates Ptch1, unleashing Smo's activity and allowing the Gli transcription factors to initiate target gene transcription.
evidence: This is a fundamental mechanism of the Hh pathway, well-established in the literature.

claim: Vismodegib is an FDA-approved Smoothened inhibitor in clinical use.
source: Despite the fact that Smo has become a drug target in oncology, with an FDA-approved Smo inhibitor in clinical use (Von Hoff et al., 2009)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation to Von Hoff et al., 2009.

claim: Smoothened consists of an extracellular N-terminal region containing a cysteine rich domain (CRD), a heptahelical transmembrane segment (7TM) and an intracellular C-terminal tail.
source: Smo consists of an extracellular N-terminal region containing a cysteine rich domain (CRD), a heptahelical transmembrane segment (7TM) and an intracellular C-terminal tail (C-term) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A showing the domain structure of Smo.

claim: Smoothened belongs to the G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR) superfamily of proteins.
source: Smo belongs to the G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR) superfamily of proteins, most closely related to the Frizzled (Fz) group of Wnt receptors (Dann et al., 2001; Fredriksson et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations to Dann et al., 2001 and Fredriksson et al., 2003.

claim: Smoothened is most closely related to the Frizzled group of Wnt receptors.
source: Smo belongs to the G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR) superfamily of proteins, most closely related to the Frizzled (Fz) group of Wnt receptors (Dann et al., 2001; Fredriksson et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations to Dann et al., 2001 and Fredriksson et al., 2003.

claim: The 7TM domain of Smoothened contains a binding site for cyclopamine.
source: Previous work on Smo has largely focused on the 7TM domain, which contains a binding site for cyclopamine, a sterol-like plant alkaloid that was the foundational Hh inhibitor (Chen et al., 2002a).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation to Chen et al., 2002a.

claim: The crystal structure of the 7TM segment of Smoothened bound to a synthetic antagonist has been determined at 2.5 Å resolution.
source: The 2.5 Å crystal structure of the 7TM segment of Smo bound to a synthetic antagonist has provided a high-resolution view of this binding pocket, which is formed by the extracellular end of the 7TM helix bundle and connecting loops (Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation to Wang et al., 2013.

claim: Specific oxysterols can fully activate Hedgehog signaling in the absence of Hedgehog ligands in multiple cell types.
source: Specific oxysterols can fully activate Hh signaling in the absence of Hh ligands in multiple cell types and also induce the accumulation of Smo in the primary cilium, a trafficking step essential for Smo to activate downstream signaling (Kha et al., 2004; Corcoran and Scott, 2006; Dwyer et al., 2007; Kim et al., 2007; Rohatgi et al., 2007; Johnson et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Oxysterols induce the accumulation of Smoothened in the primary cilium.
source: Specific oxysterols can fully activate Hh signaling in the absence of Hh ligands in multiple cell types and also induce the accumulation of Smo in the primary cilium, a trafficking step essential for Smo to activate downstream signaling (Kha et al., 2004; Corcoran and Scott, 2006; Dwyer et al., 2007; Kim et al., 2007; Rohatgi et al., 2007; Johnson et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by multiple citations.

claim: 20(S)-hydroxycholesterol directly binds Smoothened in a highly stereospecific manner.
source: We previously demonstrated that a specific side-chain oxysterol, 20(S)-hydroxycholesterol (20(S)-OHC), directly binds Smo in a manner that is highly stereospecific: the enantiomer, ent-20(S)-OHC, or the epimer, 20(R)-OHC, failed to bind Smo or to activate Hh signaling (Nachtergaele et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation to Nachtergaele et al., 2012, and by data in Figure 2C showing that ent-20(S)-OHC does not compete for binding.

claim: The enantiomer ent-20(S)-OHC fails to bind Smoothened or activate Hedgehog signaling.
source: We previously demonstrated that a specific side-chain oxysterol, 20(S)-hydroxycholesterol (20(S)-OHC), directly binds Smo in a manner that is highly stereospecific: the enantiomer, ent-20(S)-OHC, or the epimer, 20(R)-OHC, failed to bind Smo or to activate Hh signaling (Nachtergaele et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation to Nachtergaele et al., 2012, and by data in Figures 2C and 4E showing lack of competition by ent-20(S)-OHC.

claim: The epimer 20(R)-OHC fails to bind Smoothened or activate Hedgehog signaling.
source: We previously demonstrated that a specific side-chain oxysterol, 20(S)-hydroxycholesterol (20(S)-OHC), directly binds Smo in a manner that is highly stereospecific: the enantiomer, ent-20(S)-OHC, or the epimer, 20(R)-OHC, failed to bind Smo or to activate Hh signaling (Nachtergaele et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation to Nachtergaele et al., 2012, and by data in Figure 2D showing that 20(R)-OHC does not compete for binding.

claim: The oxysterol binding site on Smoothened is distinct from the cyclopamine binding site.
source: While this 'oxysterol binding site' showed allosteric interactions with the canonical cyclopamine binding site, it was clearly distinct since oxysterols did not show a competitive interaction with cyclopamine (Dwyer et al., 2007; Nachtergaele et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations, and by data in Figure 2E showing that SAG and SANT-1 do not compete with 20(S)-OHC for CRD binding.

claim: The extracellular CRD of mouse Smoothened is necessary for binding to 20(S)-OHC.
source: In contrast, ΔCRD-YFP-mSmo failed to show an interaction, suggesting that the CRD was required for oxysterol binding.
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 1D showing that ΔCRD-YFP-mSmo does not bind to 20(S)-OHC beads.

claim: The extracellular CRD of mouse Smoothened is sufficient for binding to 20(S)-OHC.
source: To determine if the mSmo CRD was sufficient to bind 20(S)-OHC, we purified isolated mSmo CRD fused to the constant region of the human IgG heavy chain (mSmo CRD-Fc; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 2A showing that purified mSmo CRD-Fc binds to 20(S)-OHC beads.

claim: The C-terminal intracellular domain of Smoothened is dispensable for binding to 20(S)-OHC.
source: For both YFP-mSmo and ΔC-YFP-mSmo, this post-Golgi band was selectively captured on 20(S)-OHC beads, showing that the C-terminal intracellular domain of Smo was dispensable for this interaction (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 1D showing that ΔC-YFP-mSmo binds to 20(S)-OHC beads.

claim: The binding of mSmo CRD-Fc to 20(S)-OHC beads is saturable with a Kd of approximately 180 nM.
source: Binding of mSmo CRD-Fc to 20(S)-OHC beads was saturable (Figure 2B)
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 2B showing a binding curve with Kd ~180 nM.

claim: 20(S)-yne is approximately 10-fold more potent than 20(S)-OHC at activating Hedgehog signaling.
source: Binding could be inhibited by free 20(S)-OHC and free 20(S)-yne, the ∼10-fold more potent alkyne analog of 20(S)-OHC (Nachtergaele et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation to Nachtergaele et al., 2012.

claim: 22(S)-OHC cannot activate Hedgehog signaling.
source: However, the enantiomer ent-20(S)-OHC, the epimer 20(R)-OHC, and 22(S)-OHC (all sterols that cannot activate Hh signaling) were unable to inhibit binding (Nachtergaele et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation to Nachtergaele et al., 2012, and by data in Figure 2D showing that 22(S)-OHC does not compete for binding.

claim: SAG and SANT-1 do not inhibit the binding of mSmo CRD-Fc to 20(S)-OHC beads.
source: Ligands known to engage Smo at the cyclopamine binding site, SAG and SANT-1, failed to inhibit the binding of mSmo CRD-Fc to 20(S)-OHC beads, as did Itraconazole, a purported Smo ligand that binds to an unknown site (Figure 2E) (Chen et al., 2002a, 2002b; Kim et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 2E showing that SAG and SANT-1 do not compete with 20(S)-OHC for CRD binding.

claim: Itraconazole does not inhibit the binding of mSmo CRD-Fc to 20(S)-OHC beads.
source: Ligands known to engage Smo at the cyclopamine binding site, SAG and SANT-1, failed to inhibit the binding of mSmo CRD-Fc to 20(S)-OHC beads, as did Itraconazole, a purported Smo ligand that binds to an unknown site (Figure 2E) (Chen et al., 2002a, 2002b; Kim et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 2E showing that Itraconazole does not compete with 20(S)-OHC for CRD binding.

claim: ΔCRD-YFP-mSmo fails to activate Hedgehog target genes in response to Sonic Hedgehog.
source: In contrast, ΔCRD-YFP-mSmo failed to activate Hh target genes or to extinguish Gli3R levels in response to both Shh and 20(S)-OHC, but retained its ability to respond to SAG (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 3A showing that ΔCRD-YFP-mSmo does not induce Gli1 expression in response to Shh.

claim: ΔCRD-YFP-mSmo fails to activate Hedgehog target genes in response to 20(S)-OHC.
source: In contrast, ΔCRD-YFP-mSmo failed to activate Hh target genes or to extinguish Gli3R levels in response to both Shh and 20(S)-OHC, but retained its ability to respond to SAG (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 3A showing that ΔCRD-YFP-mSmo does not induce Gli1 expression in response to 20(S)-OHC.

claim: ΔCRD-YFP-mSmo retains its ability to respond to SAG.
source: In contrast, ΔCRD-YFP-mSmo failed to activate Hh target genes or to extinguish Gli3R levels in response to both Shh and 20(S)-OHC, but retained its ability to respond to SAG (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 3A showing that ΔCRD-YFP-mSmo induces Gli1 expression in response to SAG.

claim: SAG-activated ΔCRD-YFP-mSmo remains susceptible to inhibition by cyclopamine.
source: SAG activated ΔCRD-YFP-mSmo remained susceptible to inhibition by cyclopamine, consistent with an intact 7TM site (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 3C showing that cyclopamine inhibits SAG-activated ΔCRD-YFP-mSmo.

claim: ΔCRD-YFP-mSmo demonstrates a higher level of basal activity in Hedgehog reporter assays.
source: As noted previously, ΔCRD-YFP-mSmo was not constitutively active, but it did demonstrate a higher level of basal activity in Hh reporter assays (Taipale et al., 2002; Aanstad et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations to Taipale et al., 2002 and Aanstad et al., 2009.

claim: Full-length Drosophila Smoothened does not bind to 20(S)-OHC beads.
source: Both full-length Drosophila melanogaster Smo (dSmo) and the isolated dSmo CRD failed to bind 20(S)-OHC beads.
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 4A-B showing that dSmo does not bind to 20(S)-OHC beads.

claim: The isolated Drosophila Smoothened CRD does not bind to 20(S)-OHC beads.
source: Both full-length Drosophila melanogaster Smo (dSmo) and the isolated dSmo CRD failed to bind 20(S)-OHC beads.
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 4B showing that dSmo CRD does not bind to 20(S)-OHC beads.

claim: A truncated version of zebrafish Smoothened lacking the intracellular C-terminal region binds to 20(S)-OHC beads.
source: However, a truncated version of zebrafish Smo (zSmo) lacking the intracellular C-terminal region (YFP-zSmoΔC), expressed in mammalian cells and solubilized with detergent, bound to 20(S)-OHC beads, showing that this interaction is likely conserved in the vertebrate (but not in the invertebrate) Hh pathway.
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 4A showing that zSmoΔC binds to 20(S)-OHC beads.

claim: The oxysterol-CRD interaction is conserved in the vertebrate Hedgehog pathway.
source: However, a truncated version of zebrafish Smo (zSmo) lacking the intracellular C-terminal region (YFP-zSmoΔC), expressed in mammalian cells and solubilized with detergent, bound to 20(S)-OHC beads, showing that this interaction is likely conserved in the vertebrate (but not in the invertebrate) Hh pathway.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4A showing that both mouse and zebrafish Smo bind to 20(S)-OHC beads.

claim: The oxysterol-CRD interaction is not conserved in the invertebrate Hedgehog pathway.
source: However, a truncated version of zebrafish Smo (zSmo) lacking the intracellular C-terminal region (YFP-zSmoΔC), expressed in mammalian cells and solubilized with detergent, bound to 20(S)-OHC beads, showing that this interaction is likely conserved in the vertebrate (but not in the invertebrate) Hh pathway.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4A-B showing that Drosophila Smo does not bind to 20(S)-OHC beads.

claim: 20(S)-OHC treatment of zebrafish embryos increases expression of the Hedgehog target gene engrailed2a.
source: As expected, cyclopamine treatment suppressed expression of the reporter gene; by contrast, 20(S)-OHC treated embryos showed a significant increase in the number of GFP positive fast twitch muscles compared to vehicle treated embryos (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1 showing increased eng2a:GFP expression in 20(S)-OHC treated embryos.

claim: 20(S)-OHC treatment of zebrafish embryos expands the expression domain of the endogenous Hedgehog target gene ptch2.
source: Consistent with this, 20(S)-OHC treated embryos also showed a modest expansion of the expression domain of the endogenous Hh target gene, ptch2.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4C demonstrating expanded ptch2 expression in 20(S)-OHC treated embryos.

claim: Cyclopamine treatment of zebrafish embryos suppresses expression of the Hedgehog target gene engrailed2a.
source: As expected, cyclopamine treatment suppressed expression of the reporter gene
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1 showing decreased eng2a:GFP expression in cyclopamine treated embryos.

claim: The binding of zebrafish Smo ectodomain to 20(S)-OHC beads is saturable with a Kd of approximately 170 nM.
source: The zSmo ectodomain demonstrated saturable, specific binding to 20(S)-OHC beads (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 4D showing a binding curve with Kd ~170 nM.

claim: The zebrafish Smo ectodomain structure includes residues 41-158.
source: Refinement resulted in an R-factor of 21.6% (R-free: 26.0%) with two zSmo molecules in the crystallographic asymmetric unit, each composed of a well-defined model that included residues 41–158
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by the crystallographic data in Table 1.

claim: The N- and C-terminal regions of the zebrafish Smo ectodomain could not be traced due to missing electron density.
source: Although we set-up crystallization trials with the entire zSmo ectodomain (residues 29–212), the N- and C-terminal regions could not be traced due to missing electron density and thus were not included in the final model (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The zebrafish Smo CRD adopts a globular fold composed of four α helices and a short two-stranded β sheet.
source: The zSmo CRD monomer adopts a globular fold composed of four α helices (α1: residues Q77-N92; α2: P94-Y108; α3: Q122-N130; α3′: S133-E138) and a short two-stranded β sheet (β1: K43-S45 and β2: K116-E118; Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure Supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 5A showing the structure of the zSmo CRD.

claim: The zebrafish Smo CRD structure is stabilized by five disulfide bridges.
source: This arrangement is stabilized by five disulfide bridges (labeled *, I, II, III, IV in Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 5A showing the disulfide bridges in the zSmo CRD structure.

claim: Four out of five disulfide bridges in the zebrafish Smo CRD are highly conserved in Frizzled-like CRDs.
source: Strikingly, 4 out of 5 disulfide bridges are highly conserved (I, II, III, and IV), retaining the overall fold of the helix bundle.
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 5A and Figure 5C-E showing conserved disulfide bridges across CRD structures.

claim: The closest structural relatives of the zebrafish Smo CRD are the CRDs of Frizzled 8, secreted Frizzled-related protein 3, and muscle-specific kinase.
source: Structure-based evolutionary analysis of zSmo CRD revealed that the closest structural relatives are the CRDs of Frizzled 8 (Fz8; Dann et al., 2001; Janda et al., 2012), secreted Frizzled-related protein 3 (sFRP3, Dann et al., 2001) and muscle-specific kinase (MuSK, Stiegler et al., 2009), shown clustered in the blue branch in Figure 5B (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 5B showing the phylogenetic tree of CRD structures.

claim: Purified zebrafish Smo ectodomain behaves as a monomer in solution at low concentration.
source: In agreement with this crystal packing analysis, purified zSmo ectodomain behaved as a monomer in solution at low concentration (5 µM) when assessed using multi angle light scattering (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D showing MALS data indicating monomeric behavior.

claim: The most prominent groove in the zebrafish Smo CRD structure is located at an equivalent position to the Frizzled 8 palmitoleyl-binding groove.
source: To investigate the putative oxysterol binding site in the Smo CRD, we calculated the volumes of potential binding pockets in our zSmo CRD structure. The most prominent groove is indeed located at an equivalent position to the Fz8 palmitoleyl-binding groove (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 6A-B showing the comparison of binding grooves in zSmo and Fz8 CRDs.

claim: The residues forming the oxysterol-binding groove in the zebrafish Smo CRD are highly conserved in all vertebrate Smo CRDs.
source: The residues forming this groove are highly conserved in all vertebrate Smo CRDs (Figure 6C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 6C showing conservation of residues in the binding groove.

claim: The volume of the oxysterol-binding groove in the zebrafish Smo CRD is 551 Å³.
source: the volume (551 Å3) and shape of the groove is sufficient for 20(S)-OHC binding.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on computational analysis of the crystal structure.

claim: Computational docking shows that the hydrophobic groove on the zebrafish Smo CRD surface can accommodate 20(S)-OHC with a favorable free energy of binding.
source: Computational docking using AutoDock (Morris et al., 2009) showed that the hydrophobic groove on the zSmo CRD surface (Figure 6A) can accommodate 20(S)-OHC with a favorable free energy of binding (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B showing the docked structure with estimated free binding energy of −9.0 kcal/mol.

claim: Mouse Smo mutations L112A, L112D, G115F, L116A, Y134F, G166F, P168A, and F170A substantially reduce binding to 20(S)-OHC beads.
source: In contrast, mutations in residues that frame the putative oxysterol pocket (L112A, L112D, G115F, L116A, Y134F, G166F, P168A, F170A) substantially reduced binding to 20(S)-OHC beads (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 2 showing reduced binding for these mutants.

claim: Mouse Smo mutations E162A, P120A/E/G, P128S/E/R, P88N, and L150A/D/S do not disrupt binding to 20(S)-OHC beads.
source: Mutations in residues on the opposite face of the putative sterol binding pocket (E162A, P120A/E/G, P128S/E/R, P88N, L150A/D/S) or at the periphery of the pocket (R165A/E and N118A) did not disrupt binding to 20(S)-OHC beads (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 2 showing preserved binding for these mutants.

claim: Mouse Smo mutations R165A/E and N118A do not disrupt binding to 20(S)-OHC beads.
source: Mutations in residues on the opposite face of the putative sterol binding pocket (E162A, P120A/E/G, P128S/E/R, P88N, L150A/D/S) or at the periphery of the pocket (R165A/E and N118A) did not disrupt binding to 20(S)-OHC beads (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 2 showing preserved binding for these mutants.

claim: Mouse Smo Y134F is completely unresponsive to 20(S)-OHC in Hedgehog reporter assays.
source: All three mutants were responsive to SAG, showing that they were not disabled, but demonstrated substantially reduced 20(S)-OHC binding and responsiveness, with the mSmo Y134F being completely unresponsive (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 6F showing no response of Y134F to 20(S)-OHC.

claim: Mouse Smo Y134F retains responsiveness to SAG.
source: All three mutants were responsive to SAG, showing that they were not disabled
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 6F showing that Y134F responds to SAG.

claim: Sonic Hedgehog-responsiveness is significantly reduced in mouse Smo Y134F and P168A mutants.
source: Interestingly, Shh-responsiveness was unaffected in mSmo G115F but significantly reduced in both mSmo Y134F and P168A.
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 6F showing reduced Shh response for Y134F and P168A.

claim: Sonic Hedgehog-responsiveness is unaffected in mouse Smo G115F mutant.
source: Interestingly, Shh-responsiveness was unaffected in mSmo G115F but significantly reduced in both mSmo Y134F and P168A.
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 6F showing preserved Shh response for G115F.

claim: Five out of eight residues essential for vertebrate Smo interactions with oxysterols are different in Drosophila Smo.
source: 5 out of 8 residues that are essential for vertebrate Smo interactions with oxysterols (zSmo residues M86, W87, G89, Y108 and G140) are different in dSmo (corresponding dSmo residues D129, Y130, A132, F151 and F187; Figure 6—figure supplement 1D), potentially providing an explanation for why dSmo does not bind to oxysterols.
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D showing the homology model of dSmo CRD.

claim: 20(R)-yne and 20-keto-yne block the binding of mSmo CRD-Fc to 20(S)-OHC beads.
source: Both molecules blocked the binding of mSmo CRD-Fc to 20(S)-OHC beads but did not affect the binding of a fluorescent cyclopamine derivative (bodipy-cyclopamine) to Smo-expressing cells, showing that they engaged the CRD site but not the 7TM site (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 7B showing that 20(R)-yne and 20-keto-yne compete with 20(S)-OHC for CRD binding.

claim: 20(R)-yne and 20-keto-yne do not affect the binding of bodipy-cyclopamine to Smo-expressing cells.
source: Both molecules blocked the binding of mSmo CRD-Fc to 20(S)-OHC beads but did not affect the binding of a fluorescent cyclopamine derivative (bodipy-cyclopamine) to Smo-expressing cells, showing that they engaged the CRD site but not the 7TM site (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 7C showing that 20(R)-yne and 20-keto-yne do not compete with bodipy-cyclopamine binding.

claim: The alkyne group is an important structural feature required for competition with 20(S)-OHC binding to the Smo CRD.
source: The alkyne group was an important structural feature required for competition, as both 20(R)-OHC and 20-keto-cholesterol (Figure 7A) failed to inhibit the CRD–20(S)-OHC interaction (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 7B showing that 20(R)-OHC and 20-keto-cholesterol do not compete for binding.

claim: 20(R)-yne and 20-keto-yne are weak activators of signaling in the absence of Sonic Hedgehog.
source: Despite binding to the mSmo CRD, 20(R)-yne and 20-keto-yne were weak activators of signaling in the absence of Shh, reinforcing the importance of stereochemistry at position 20 for Smo activation (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 7D showing weak activation by 20(R)-yne and 20-keto-yne.

claim: 20(R)-yne and 20-keto-yne inhibit signaling induced by Sonic Hedgehog.
source: However, both molecules inhibited signaling induced by the native ligand Shh, the CRD agonist 20(S)-OHC or the 7TM agonist SAG (Figure 8A–C and Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 8C showing inhibition of Shh-induced signaling by 20(R)-yne and 20-keto-yne.

claim: 20(R)-yne and 20-keto-yne inhibit signaling induced by 20(S)-OHC.
source: However, both molecules inhibited signaling induced by the native ligand Shh, the CRD agonist 20(S)-OHC or the 7TM agonist SAG (Figure 8A–C and Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 8B showing inhibition of 20(S)-OHC-induced signaling by 20(R)-yne and 20-keto-yne.

claim: 20(R)-yne and 20-keto-yne inhibit signaling induced by SAG.
source: However, both molecules inhibited signaling induced by the native ligand Shh, the CRD agonist 20(S)-OHC or the 7TM agonist SAG (Figure 8A–C and Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 8A showing inhibition of SAG-induced signaling by 20(R)-yne and 20-keto-yne.

claim: 20(R)-yne and 20-keto-yne reduce signaling by constitutively active, oncogenic mSmoM2.
source: Both the molecules also reduced signaling by mSmoM2, a constitutively active, oncogenic Smo mutant (Taipale et al., 2000), and mSmo D477H, the mouse version of a human Smo mutant that is resistant to the FDA-approved drug Vismodegib (Figure 8D,E) (Yauch et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 8E showing inhibition of mSmoM2 signaling by 20(R)-yne and 20-keto-yne.

claim: 20(R)-yne and 20-keto-yne reduce signaling by mSmo D477H, a Vismodegib-resistant mutant.
source: Both the molecules also reduced signaling by mSmoM2, a constitutively active, oncogenic Smo mutant (Taipale et al., 2000), and mSmo D477H, the mouse version of a human Smo mutant that is resistant to the FDA-approved drug Vismodegib (Figure 8D,E) (Yauch et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 8D showing inhibition of mSmo D477H signaling by 20(R)-yne and 20-keto-yne.

claim: 20(R)-yne and 20-keto-yne are CRD-targeted partial agonists of Smoothened.
source: We hereafter call these molecules oxysterol-based inhibitors or OBIs. This activity profile shows that the OBIs are CRD-targeted partial agonists of Smo that can reduce signaling by Smo activators and by clinically relevant Smo mutants.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on the combined data showing weak activation but strong inhibition of Smo signaling.

claim: 20(R)-yne and 20-keto-yne induce Smoothened accumulation in cilia when added alone.
source: The CRD-targeted OBIs both behaved like cyclopamine in this assay—they induced Smo accumulation in cilia when added alone and also did not block Shh-induced ciliary accumulation of Smo (Figure 8F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 8F showing ciliary Smo accumulation with OBI treatment.

claim: 20(R)-yne and 20-keto-yne do not block Sonic Hedgehog-induced ciliary accumulation of Smoothened.
source: The CRD-targeted OBIs both behaved like cyclopamine in this assay—they induced Smo accumulation in cilia when added alone and also did not block Shh-induced ciliary accumulation of Smo (Figure 8F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 8F showing that OBIs do not prevent Shh-induced ciliary Smo accumulation.

claim: Cyclopamine induces Smoothened accumulation in cilia even in the absence of Sonic Hedgehog.
source: Cyclopamine and cyclopamine derivatives (that contain a sterol-like tetracyclic ring structure) do not block Smo ciliary accumulation (Figure 8F) and in fact can drive Smo accumulation in cilia even in the absence of Shh (Rohatgi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 8F showing ciliary Smo accumulation with cyclopamine treatment.

claim: Non-sterol 7TM antagonists like SANT-1 and Vismodegib prevent Sonic Hedgehog-induced Smoothened accumulation in cilia.
source: On the other hand, non-sterol 7TM antagonists like SANT-1 and Vismodegib prevent Shh-induced Smo accumulation in cilia (Rohatgi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation to Rohatgi et al., 2009.

claim: Cyclopamine blocks the interaction between mSmo CRD-Fc and 20(S)-OHC beads.
source: Indeed, unlike the non-sterol 7TM inhibitors (Figure 2E), cyclopamine blocked the interaction between the mSmo CRD-Fc and 20(S)-OHC beads (Figure 8G), suggesting that it is capable of binding the CRD in this in vitro assay.
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 8G showing that cyclopamine competes with 20(S)-OHC for CRD binding.

claim: Tomatidine does not block the interaction between mSmo CRD-Fc and 20(S)-OHC beads.
source: The binding of mSmo CRD-Fc to 20(S)-OHC beads can be inhibited by cyclopamine but not by the structurally-related alkaloid tomatidine.
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 8G showing that tomatidine does not compete with 20(S)-OHC for CRD binding.

claim: The Smo CRD binds to 20(S)-OHC in the region that was previously identified as the binding site for small hydrophobic molecules in other CRDs.
source: Structure-guided mutagenesis studies revealed that the Smo CRD binds to 20(S)-OHC in the region that was previously identified as the binding site for small hydrophobic molecules in other CRDs, formed by the evolutionary conserved helical bundle of the CRD core.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by the mutagenesis data in Figure 6E-F and structural comparisons in Figure 5 and Figure 6.

claim: CRDs evolved from an ancestral domain that sensed hydrophobic molecules.
source: This supports the hypothesis that CRDs evolved from an ancestral domain that sensed hydrophobic molecules (Bazan and de Sauvage, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation to Bazan and de Sauvage, 2009, and by the structural analysis showing conserved binding pockets across CRD family members.

claim: The Smo CRD oxysterol binding site is most similar to the palmitoleyl-binding site in Frizzled CRDs.
source: Our structural analysis showed that the Smo CRD oxysterol binding site is most similar to the palmitoleyl-binding site in Fz CRDs (Janda et al., 2012)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by structural comparisons in Figure 6A-B showing similar groove locations and volumes.

claim: The binding grooves in Smo CRD and Frizzled CRD are built of divergent residues.
source: however, the binding grooves are built of divergent residues (Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting that they accommodate different classes of hydrophobic ligands.
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 showing sequence alignment with different residues lining the binding grooves.

claim: There is dramatic synergy between 20(S)-OHC and SAG in activating Smoothened.
source: Indeed, while the 7TM and CRD sites are separable, the dramatic synergy between 20(S)-OHC and SAG we have previously reported suggests a positive allosteric link between these domains (Nachtergaele et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation to Nachtergaele et al., 2012.

claim: The synergy between 20(S)-OHC and SAG suggests a positive allosteric link between the CRD and 7TM domains of Smoothened.
source: Indeed, while the 7TM and CRD sites are separable, the dramatic synergy between 20(S)-OHC and SAG we have previously reported suggests a positive allosteric link between these domains (Nachtergaele et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation to Nachtergaele et al., 2012.

claim: The synergy between 20(S)-OHC and SAG implies that 7TM and CRD ligands can bind to Smoothened simultaneously.
source: This synergy also implies that 7TM and CRD ligands can bind to Smo simultaneously.
evidence: This is stated in the text as an inference from the observed synergy between the two ligands.

claim: Oxysterols do not decrease the binding of bodipy-cyclopamine to cells expressing full-length Smoothened.
source: This result was unexpected because oxysterols do not decrease the binding of bodipy-cyclopamine to cells expressing full-length Smo (Figure 7C and Dwyer et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 7C showing that oxysterols do not compete with bodipy-cyclopamine binding.

claim: Cyclopamine has a high affinity (Kd ~10 nM) binding site in the 7TM domain of Smoothened.
source: We believe that this discrepancy is due to the fact that the cell-based bodipy-cyclopamine binding assay is mostly measuring the interaction between cyclopamine and its high affinity (Kd∼10 nM, Rominger et al., 2009) binding site in the 7TM domain.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation to Rominger et al., 2009.

claim: Cyclopamine is a sterol that induces the accumulation of Smoothened in primary cilia.
source: As noted above, cyclopamine is a sterol that induces the accumulation of Smo in primary cilia, both properties that distinguish it from the pure 7TM site inhibitors SANT-1 and Vismodegib.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 8F showing ciliary Smo accumulation with cyclopamine treatment.

claim: Some mutations in the Smo CRD that abolish oxysterol binding also substantially dampen the ability of Sonic Hedgehog to activate Smoothened.
source: Some mutations (Smo Y134F, P168A) that abolish 20(S)-OHC responses do indeed substantially dampen the ability of Shh to activate Smo.
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 6F showing reduced Shh responsiveness for Y134F and P168A mutants.

claim: The simple inversion of stereochemistry at C-20 converts a potent Smoothened agonist into a weak partial agonist and an effective inhibitor of signaling.
source: Remarkably, the simple inversion of the stereochemistry at C-20 converts a potent agonist into a weak partial agonist and an effective inhibitor of signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figures 7D and 8A-C showing that 20(R)-yne is a weak activator but strong inhibitor.

claim: Smoothened activation potential depends critically on the spatial orientation between the ring system and the iso-octyl chain of 20(S)-OHC.
source: The structures of the OBIs suggest that Smo activation potential depends critically on the spatial orientation between the ring system and the iso-octyl chain of 20(S)-OHC.
evidence: This is stated in the text as an inference from the structure-activity relationships observed with different stereoisomers.

claim: Partial agonists offer the possibility of blocking unrestrained signaling while preserving lower-level, physiological signaling.
source: Partial agonists offer the possibility of blocking unrestrained signaling (such as that seen in cancer) while preserving lower-level, physiological signaling (Riese, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation to Riese, 2011.

claim: Currently used Smoothened antagonists cause significant side-effects, leading nearly half of patients in some trials to discontinue treatment.
source: This ability to attenuate Smo activity may be useful since currently used Smo antagonists cause significant side-effects, leading nearly half of the patients in some trials to discontinue treatment (Tang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation to Tang et al., 2012.
